extracted.intended_audience: USCIS/DHS adjudicators, immigration practitioners, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether an alien is inadmissible as likely to become a public charge under the DHS Totality of Circumstances framework, including factor-by-factor considerations, weighting rules, examples, valuation methodology for monetizable benefits, and public charge bond procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which an alien’s age makes the alien more or less likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive finding: 18 ≤ age ≤ 61. Negative findings: Age > 61 unless the alien can demonstrate employment or sufficient household assets and resources; Age < 18 unless the alien can demonstrate employment or sufficient household assets and resources. Use age to assess likelihood of future self-support in the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the alien’s health makes the alien more or less likely to become a public charge, including whether the alien has been diagnosed with a medical condition that is likely to require extensive medical treatment or institutionalization or that will interfere with the alien’s ability to provide and care for him- or herself, to attend school, or to work upon admission or adjustment of status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive: Absence of any medical conditions likely to require extensive treatment/institutionalization or to interfere with self-care, schooling, or working. Negative: Presence of any such medical condition. Heavily weighed negative: diagnosed condition likely to require extensive treatment/institutionalization or to interfere with work/school/self-care combined with being uninsured and having neither the prospect of obtaining private health insurance nor financial resources to pay for reasonably foreseeable medical costs related to the condition. Examples and case narratives illustrate that untreated Class B conditions plus lack of insurance/resources can be heavily weighted against admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family Status (household size/support)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the alien’s household size and family support relationships make the alien more or less likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the alien has a household that he/she supports, whether another household is supporting the alien, and household size in relation to household assets/resources. The table notes empirical context (e.g., larger families have higher non-cash assistance rates). Examples: a single-person household with sufficient income/assets is positive; being dependent in a large household with insufficient resources is negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assets, Resources, and Financial Status
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the alien’s household income, assets, and resources make the alien more or less likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations to evaluate: annual gross household income excluding public benefits; additional income from non-household individuals who reside with the alien; ongoing outside income; household cash assets (12 months of checking/savings statements); non-cash assets convertible to cash within 12 months (e.g., net cash value of real estate minus loans, annuities, securities, retirement and educational accounts); financial liabilities; applications for or receipt of public benefits (on/after effective date); certification/approval to receive public benefits (on/after effective date); applications/receipt of immigration fee waivers (on/after effective date); credit history/score; private health insurance or resources to pay foreseeable medical costs. Weighting thresholds and examples: Heavily weighed positive if household assets/resources ≥ 250% of FPG for household size or alien is authorized to work and employed with annual household income ≥ 250% FPG. Heavily weighed negatives include inability to demonstrate current employment/employment history/reasonable prospect of future employment; currently receiving one or more public benefits (8 CFR 212.21(b)); received one or more public benefits within 36 months immediately preceding filing; diagnosed medical condition likely to require extensive treatment and uninsured with no prospect of private insurance/resources; prior public-charge-based inadmissibility/deportability. Positive examples: annual gross household income ≥ 125% of FPG for household size, or household assets ≥ 5 times the difference between total household income and 125% FPG; sufficient assets/resources to cover foreseeable medical costs; good credit; private health insurance. Negative examples: assets/resources < 125% of FPG (or < 5x difference), insufficient assets for foreseeable medical costs, applied for/received public benefits on/after effective date, approved for public benefits, received immigration fee waiver on/after effective date, bad credit/low score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and Skills
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the alien has adequate education and skills to obtain or maintain employment sufficient to avoid becoming a public charge if authorized for employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations: employment history; high school diploma or higher education; occupational skills, certifications, or licenses; proficiency in English or additional languages. Positive findings: adequate education/skills to obtain/maintain employment, sufficient language proficiency to enter the U.S. job market, ability to obtain skilled or higher-paid labor. Negative findings: no employment history, lack of high school diploma or higher education, inadequate education/skills to obtain/maintain employment, insufficient English to enter the job market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support (sponsor evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponsor’s demonstrated financial ability and willingness to support the alien via an affidavit of support, when required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider sponsor’s annual income, assets, resources; sponsor’s relationship to the applicant; and the likelihood the sponsor would actually provide financial support. Positive: sponsor’s assets/resources ≥ 125% of the most recent Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG) based on sponsor household size; likely the sponsor would provide support. Negative: unlikely sponsor would provide support. Weighting/disqualifying rule: Assets/resources < 125% of FPG for sponsor household size is disqualifying/inadmissible for applicants subject to sponsor requirements. Analysis note: a required but absent or insufficient affidavit of support will lead to an inadmissibility finding; otherwise no single factor (other than the required but absent/insufficient affidavit) alone establishes inadmissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective Immigration Status and Period of Stay
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the alien’s prospective immigration status and anticipated period of stay make the alien more or less likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the category of admission or adjustment (e.g., employment-based vs family-based; intended period of stay) affects likelihood of self-sufficiency. Examples in illustrative tables: applying under an employment-based adjustment category was considered a positive factor for Applicant A; family-based adjustment (parent of U.S. citizen) shown as neutral in examples. Use item as a factor in totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the Circumstances Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The overall analytic process: evaluate all enumerated factors and circumstances and determine whether positives outweigh negatives to conclude admissibility or inadmissibility for public charge purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: evaluate all factors/circumstances within each factor; the mere presence of any one enumerated circumstance is not alone determinative (except absence/insufficiency of required affidavit of support); assess whether each factor is positive (decreases likelihood of becoming a public charge) or negative (increases likelihood); assess the degree to which each factor is positive or negative — weight depends on facts and relation to other factors; identify heavily weighed factors (certain enumerated factors generally weigh heavily for or against public-charge findings). Outcome rules: Admissible if positive factors/circumstances outweigh negatives such that alien is not likely to receive public benefits in the future (as defined in 8 CFR 212.21(b)). Inadmissible if negatives outweigh positives such that alien is likely to receive public benefits in the future. Agencies may issue RFE/NOID to give applicants opportunity to rebut or provide additional evidence; examples illustrate application of totality approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting of Factors and Heavily Weighed Criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on how to weigh individual factors in the public charge determination and which circumstances are generally given heavy weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule: other than heavily weighed factors, weight given to an individual factor generally depends on particular facts/circumstances and its relationship to other factors. Enumerated heavily weighed positives include: household assets/resources ≥ 250% of FPG for household size; alien authorized to work and employed with annual household income ≥ 250% of FPG. Enumerated heavily weighed negatives include: inability to demonstrate current employment/employment history or reasonable prospect of future employment; current receipt of one or more public benefits as defined in 8 CFR 212.21(b); receipt of public benefits within 36 months preceding filing; diagnosed medical condition likely to require extensive treatment or institutionalization or that will interfere with ability to work/attend school/self-care combined with being uninsured and lacking prospect of private insurance/resources; prior findings of inadmissibility/deportability on public-charge grounds. Note: except for required but absent/insufficient sponsor affidavit, no single factor alone establishes admissibility/inadmissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation of Monetizable Public Benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodology for establishing a monetary value for certain monetizable public benefits to determine whether the alien (or household share attributable to the alien) exceeds thresholds such as the 15 percent threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic approach: For benefits provided on a household basis, DHS/USCIS will consider only the portion attributable to the alien by prorating the benefit among eligible household members. Cash benefits: calculate the amount attributable to the alien in proportion to other household members (e.g., $600 shared among 3 eligible individuals = $200 attributed to the alien). SNAP: calculate annual aggregate amount attributable to the alien based on monthly amounts deposited to the EBT account and divide by number of eligible household members (based on the alien’s reporting). Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher and Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance: calculate proportional value attributable to the eligible alien by dividing the amount of the benefit by the number of people receiving it. DHS invites public comment and data on these approaches and on alternatives such as assigning value using HUD rules at 24 CFR 5.520.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Charge Bonds (posting, breach, monitoring, cancellation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures and purpose for public charge bonds for adjustment of status applicants: bonds intended to hold the United States and jurisdictions harmless against aliens becoming public charges and may permit admission despite a public-charge inadmissibility finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overview: Public charge bonds are issued on the condition the alien does not become a public charge; if the alien admitted after posting a bond becomes a public charge, the bond is breached regardless of whether payment was demanded. Historical procedures summarized: consular officer would advise immigrant visa applicants in writing of bond amount; a public charge bond historically had to be at least $1,000; INS/USCIS monitored bonds periodically (reviews every 5 years if no request to cancel); interested parties could request review/cancellation and INS would notify alien and allow evidence to show bond not breached; upon breach, obligor required to pay actual expenses within timeframes and remaining amounts could be extracted from the bond (ex: payment required within 30 days, then bond applied). Current context: USCIS rarely exercises bonding authority post-IIRIRA; ICE Form I-352 references public charge bonds though ICE does not administer them. Relationship to Affidavit of Support: bonds are distinct but complementary to affidavits of support; both are means to recover costs associated with receipt of public benefits. Regulatory citations: 8 CFR 103.6, 8 CFR 213.1; AFM Chapter 61.1 guidance referenced.
